title: 4 Quality Assurance Traps to Avoid
author: Mr. Nickhart
summary: This article by Mr. Nickhart maps four persistent traps in school quality assurance and proposes four alternative frameworks for thinking about it. The first trap is framing QA as a question of 'how good is it?' — a framing that privileges the observer's existing biases and mistakes performance for learning, since real learning is largely invisible and only detectable far downstream from instruction. The second trap is noticing change too late: school quality can degrade imperceptibly over time, and waiting for test results means feedback on curriculum and pedagogy arrives well after the damage is done. The third trap is believing leaders possess absolute truth — in fact, causal chains in schools are multiply determined, data is inherently unreliable, and those closest to a problem (teachers, TAs, ECTs) consistently hold more accurate diagnoses than those whose very presence distorts what they observe. The fourth trap is treating school culture and climate as separate from educational outcomes, when in reality collegial dynamics, psychological safety, and how leaders communicate expectations are upstream variables that directly shape teaching quality. Against these traps, the author proposes knowledge-building (QA as inquiry, not inspection), collaborative observation (multiple lenses agreed in advance), impact-domain analysis (widening the causal aperture before attributing blame), and layered scrutiny (overview vs. depth, each with its own purpose).
points: The question 'How good is it?' is structurally flawed as a QA driver because it triggers confirmation bias, rewards familiarity with preferred strategies, and mistakes visible engagement for actual learning — which is invisible and temporally distant from instruction.

Learning walks and observations give leaders a skewed picture by definition: their presence changes what teachers do, so what is observed is performance under surveillance, not typical practice — making inquiry into underlying beliefs more diagnostic than observation of surface actions.

The EEF's three-concept framework (buy-in, fidelity, reach) offers a more precise monitoring architecture than generic lesson observation: buy-in probes whether colleagues hold the beliefs required for a strategy to work; fidelity checks whether they implement it fully; reach identifies who is being missed.

Causal attribution in schools is inherently invalid at the individual-event level: multiple causes produce every effect and multiple effects follow every cause, so leaders who assign confident cause-and-effect narratives from single observations are engaging in motivated reasoning, not diagnosis.

Treating culture and climate as a soft side-channel to educational outcomes is a category error — colleague wellbeing, psychological safety, and leadership communication patterns are upstream variables that directly regulate teaching quality and must be integrated into any QA model.
quotes: We can only gain an insight through proxies because learning is largely invisible and happens over time. The problem is that what we might commonly look for and notice when we're doing quality assurance work are poor proxies:

Leaders can have a pretty skewed view of school life because we change others' behaviours simply by being there. It is far more useful to try and understand the underlying beliefs, assumptions and values of colleagues because they sustain actions.

While the rubric may have been helpful to draw attention to specific practices that we want teachers to work on, they can ultimately limit practice and provide us with a skewed view on the reality of school life because they could oversimplify the complex to the extent that practices lacks nuance and responsiveness.
Catching misconceptions early through checking for understanding here can help leaders to intervene before habits become embedded and time is lost.
We can only learn what we think about and we can only think about what we are paying attention to, so as early warning systems go, attention is first pick.

Not only are measurements of learning likely to be unreliable, but, as Muller argues, the practice of measuring itself can have negative effects on climate. Muller talks of a toxic cycle measuring leading to mistrust and mistrust leading to more measurement. All the more reason to focus more on mapping, rather than weighing.

It is often the person closes to the problem that has the most useful insights - leaders are often removed from the reality of problems because they influence others with their very presences and truth does not often rise to the top.
We must treat our assumptions as hypotheses to be tested rather than truths to be confirmed.
